passages.happening:
The man praises his bride. ‘Your eyes are like doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead’ (verse 1). ‘Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn sheep coming up from the washing; each has its twin, and not one of them is lost’ (verse 2). ‘Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your mouth is lovely’ (verse 3). ‘Your neck is like the tower of David, built with rows of stones’ (verse 4).

He goes on, in images of fawns and lilies, and then stops, turning to a picture of a mountain of myrrh and a hill of frankincense (verses 5-6). ‘You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with the king crowned on his wedding day. Chapter 4 continues the wedding. For the first time he calls her his bride, a name that comes six times between 4:8 and 5:1 and nowhere else. For many readers this is the wedding night told in poetry.

Verses 1 to 7 are a love poem that praises the beloved part by part, a form scholars sometimes call by the Arabic word wasf. The Song has four of them. To a modern reader some images sound odd, but each makes one point. Goats streaming down Gilead picture dark, flowing hair, since the goats there were black. Teeth like newly shorn sheep, each with its twin, praise white, even teeth, in a world where many adults had lost some. The tower of David pictures upright bearing. The images are meant to be felt, not pictured literally.

The poem moves downward and then stops with restraint. It is framed by the same praise at its start and end: how beautiful you are, altogether beautiful.
passages.later: Gilead was known for its flocks: ‘Gilead is Mine’, God says of that land (Psalm 60:7). And the Bible's first word about the body stands behind this praise: ‘And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good’ (Genesis 1:31).
passages.hard:
How should a reader today handle the chapter's frank praise of the body?

The chapter praises a woman's beauty in physical detail, and some readers find that embarrassing in Scripture. Several points help.

First, the language is poetic and restrained. It uses images rather than explicit description, and it treats the body with admiration, not crudeness. Second, the setting is a wedding: the man calls the woman his bride, so the praise belongs within the covenant of marriage. Third, the Bible does not treat the body as shameful. God made it and called it good, and Genesis 2 ends with the man and woman naked and unashamed.

Allegorical readers, ancient and modern, have often read the imagery as describing the beauty of God's people, and some have been uneasy with a literal reading. Many readers today think the literal and the spiritual readings can stand together: the chapter honors married love and the body as God's good gifts, and in doing so it points beyond itself. The Song speaks about the body in a way that is neither coy nor coarse, but grateful.
passages.asks: He sees her and says she is altogether beautiful. If you are married, ask how freely you tell your husband or wife what you delight in about them. And whoever you are, ask how you have learned to see your own body: as God's good work, or as something to hide.

passages.t: A garden locked up, and the bride's invitation
passages.happening:
“Come with me from Lebanon, my bride, come with me from Lebanon!” (verse 8). Come down from the peaks of Amana, Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards.

‘You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes’ (verse 9). “How delightful is your love, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine” (verse 10).

‘My sister, my bride, you are a garden locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed’ (verse 12). He pictures her as an orchard of pomegranates, full of the finest spices (verses 13-14), ‘a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon’ (verse 15).

Then she answers: ‘Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices. Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon are the mountains of the far north: remote, rugged, home to wild animals. He pictures her as far off and wild, and calls her to come to him.

‘Sister’ was a common word of affection for a beloved in ancient love poetry, including Egyptian love songs, where lovers call each other sister and brother. It has nothing to do with family relation.

A private garden in the ancient world was walled and locked, and a sealed spring was kept for its owner. The locked garden pictures a love kept for one person. The spices, nard and cinnamon from far to the east, with saffron, calamus, myrrh and aloes, describe a garden of unimaginable riches.

Notice the words in verse 16. She first calls it her own garden, and then, in the same breath, his garden. The garden is opened by her own invitation. Her gift of herself is freely given.
passages.later: Proverbs uses the same pictures for faithful married love: ‘Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well’ (Proverbs 5:15). And the law names Hermon by the name used here: it is the mountain ‘the Amorites call Senir’ (Deuteronomy 3:9).
passages.asks: The garden is locked and opened only by her own invitation. Ask how you honor the freedom of the person you love, never taking what is not freely given. And ask what it would mean to keep your love for one person, as the garden is kept.
